text: Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) is the flag carrier of Pakistan, with its primary hub at Jinnah International Airport in Karachi, and secondary hubs at Allama Iqbal International Airport in Lahore and Islamabad International Airport. PIA was under the administrative control of the Secretary to the Government of Pakistan for Aviation until its privatization in 2025. The airline traces its origins to Orient Airways, founded on 29 October 1946 by Mirza Ahmad Ispahani and Adamjee Haji Dawood in Calcutta, British India, and became the first and only Muslim-owned airline in the British Raj. After Pakistan's independence on 14 August 1947, Orient Airways began relief operations and served routes between East and West Pakistan. In 1952, the government subsidized Orient Airways by purchasing three Lockheed L-1049 Super Constellations through a newly established subsidiary, Pakistan International Airlines (PIA), at a cost of 25 million rupees. On 1 October 1953, Orient Airways and PIA were formally merged under the Pakistan International Airlines Corporation Ordinance, 1955, with the government taking majority control. The merged airline operated a fleet of three Super Constellations, two Convair CV-240s, and eleven DC-3s. On 11 March 1955, Orient Airways ceased operations. PIA inaugurated its first international route on 11 March 1955, flying from Karachi to London Heathrow via Cairo and Rome using Super Constellations, carrying 113,165 passengers in 1955—50% more than in 1954. In May 1956, PIA ordered five Vickers Viscount 815s and partnered with Pan Am to train personnel. Passenger numbers rose to 208,000 between 1957 and 1958, prompting the purchase of two additional Super Constellations. In February 1960, PIA wet-leased a Boeing 707 from Pan American Airlines and introduced it on the Karachi-London route on 7 March 1960, becoming the second Asian airline to operate a jet aircraft commercially, with an all-Pakistani crew beginning operations on 20 June 1960. By the end of 1960, PIA achieved financial profitability. On 5 May 1961, it launched its first trans-Atlantic route, Karachi to New York JFK via London, which was suspended in February 1963. In 1961, PIA ordered three Boeing 720s, delivered in 1962. On 2 January 1962, a PIA Boeing 720B set a world record speed of 938.78 km/h (582.98 mph) from London to Karachi, a record still held today. In 1963, Fokker F27 Friendships and Sikorsky helicopters were ordered; the latter served 20 towns in East Pakistan until 1966. In 1964, PIA began flying the Dhaka-Guangzhou-Shanghai route, becoming the first non-Communist airline to fly to China, and on 10 May 1964, became the first non-Soviet airline to offer flights to Europe via Moscow. During the Indo-Pakistani War of 1965, PIA's aircraft were used for military logistics. The Viscounts were phased out in 1966 and replaced by four Hawker Siddeley Tridents. PIA expanded its network in the 1960s, adding Dhahran in 1962, Cairo services resumed, and by 1966, Paris, Istanbul, Baghdad, Kuwait, Jeddah, and Nairobi were added. Bangkok was added in 1967, and Manila, Tokyo, and Damascus in 1969. On 11 May 1967, Air Marshal Asghar Khan announced that PIA had become the fifth largest profit-making airline in the world, carrying one million passengers annually. In July 1967, he announced plans to build 64-room hotels in Sylhet, Sargodha, Sukkur, Mohenjo-daro, Chitral, Gilgit, and Kaptai, and 88-room hotels in Khulna, Lyallpur, Multan, and Murree, with 20 cottages attached to the 644-room Kaptai Hotel, and 125-room hotels in Peshawar and Chittagong. These European-style motels, equipped with air conditioning, heating, parking, and swimming pools, were completed in 1970 and funded through private investment, with no government financial participation. A new holding company was established to attract domestic investment, and Pakistan Services Ltd. contributed significantly. Bechtel Corp. prepared the design and cost estimates, recommending standardized designs using local materials. On 3 December 1971, a French national's attempt to hijack a PIA flight from Paris to Karachi was thwarted by French security forces. Transatlantic flights to New York resumed in May 1972 with a European stopover. In 1972, PIA added Tripoli to its network following improved ties with Libya and leased two Boeing 707s to Yugoslav airline JAT (now Air Serbia). In 1973, PIA acquired McDonnell Douglas DC-10s to replace its Boeing 707-300s. Nur Khan was appointed PIA executive for a second term in 1974, and in 1974, PIA launched Pakistan International Cargo. In 1976, PIA leased its first two Boeing 747s from TAP Air Portugal. By 1976–7, PIA carried 2.2 million passengers, up from 698,000 in 1972–3, and revenues reached $134 million in July–December 1976. On 20 January 1978, a PIA Fokker 27 was hijacked en route to Karachi from Sukkur. PIA began providing technical and administrative assistance or leasing aircraft to foreign airlines including Air China, Air Malta, Choson Minhang (now Air Koryo), Philippine Airlines, Somali Airlines, and Yemenia. A PIA subsidiary also began offering hotel management services in the UAE. Political upheaval in Pakistan during the late 1970s negatively impacted PIA's operations. In the 1980s, PIA expanded operations with the opening of a cargo handling center at Karachi airport, duty-free shops, the first C and D safety checks on its fleet, and the introduction of its first Airbus A300B4-200. In 1981, PIA had nearly 24,000 employees, which declined to 20,000 by 1983, still maintaining the world's highest employee-to-aircraft ratio. Operations became increasingly decentralized during the early 1980s. PIA reported its highest ever profits in 1981–82 and again in 1983–84. In 1984, PIA introduced the Night Coach service as a low-cost domestic alternative. The PIA Planetarium was inaugurated in Karachi, followed by ones in Lahore and Peshawar, featuring retired PIA aircraft for educational use. Two retired Boeing 720B aircraft were donated to the Karachi and Lahore planetaria. PIA profits rose again in 1984–85. In June 1985, PIA became the first Asian airline to operate the Boeing 737-300, after six aircraft were delivered. PIA played a key role in establishing Emirates in 1985 by providing technical and administrative support, leasing a Boeing 737–300 and an Airbus A300B4-200. In late 1987 and early 1988, services to Malé, Manchester, and Toronto were introduced. Throughout the 1990s, PIA sustained operating losses and liquidity problems due to frequent pilot strikes, vendor issues, over-staffing, and political interference. In 1990, First Officer Maliha Sami became the first female pilot of PIA on the Karachi-Panjgur-Turbat-Gwadar route. In June 1991, PIA took delivery of its first of six Airbus A310-300s, introducing flights to Tashkent in 1992 and Zurich in 1993. In March 1993, AVM Farooq Umar became managing director. An Open Skies agreement between Karachi and Dubai was agreed upon in 1993, allowing 12 private airlines to operate domestically, which placed significant financial pressure on PIA. PIA operates a fleet of 32 aircraft, primarily Boeing 777 types, Airbus A320s, and ATR aircraft. It runs nearly 50 daily flights, serving 20 domestic and 28 international destinations across Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and North America. PIA operates a frequent flyer program called Awards +Plus and is not part of any airline alliance. The airline owns Sofitel Paris, The Scribe Hotel in Paris, and The Roosevelt Hotel in New York City, which is now used as a homeless shelter. The Government of Pakistan's 2020 report noted that after Air Marshals Nur Khan and Asghar Khan—whose leadership was regarded as the "Golden Age of PIA"—departed, the airline entered a downward trajectory, suffering billions in losses, with declining assets, escalating disciplinary issues, and unions indirectly taking control. Capable aircraft were grounded, and repairable equipment was neglected. From 30 June 2020 until 29 November 2024, PIA was banned from flying in European airspace after the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) determined it was not capable of certifying or overseeing its operations in accordance with international standards. This ban was also implemented in other non-EU territories after it was revealed that at least a fourth of all pilot licenses issued in Pakistan were not genuine. Following prolonged financial losses, governance issues, and international operational restrictions, PIA was privatized in 2025, ending direct government ownership and transferring majority control to the private sector.

In late 1987 and early 1988, PIA introduced services to Malé, Manchester, and Toronto. Throughout the 1990s, the airline faced sustained operating losses and liquidity problems due to frequent pilot strikes, vendor issues, over-staffing, and political interference in management. In 1990, First Officer Maliha Sami became the first female pilot of PIA when she flew the Karachi-Panjgur-Turbat-Gwadar route. In June 1991, PIA received its first of six Airbus A310-300s, which enabled the airline to launch flights to Tashkent in 1992 and Zürich in 1993. In March 1993, AVM Farooq Umar became managing director. That year, an Open Skies agreement between Karachi and Dubai was agreed upon, allowing 12 private airlines to operate domestically in Pakistan, both of which placed significant pressure on PIA’s financial performance. In 1994, PIA launched six new routes to the Persian Gulf and CIS countries and introduced a tourist 'Air Safari' scenic flight over the Karakoram Mountains. Non-stop flights from Lahore and Islamabad to JFK and Canada were introduced, and PIA added Jakarta, Fujairah, Baku, and Al-Ain to its network. The airline also became a client of SABRE, Galileo, and Amadeus. In 1996, a Tupolev Tu-154 was briefly leased to manage increased passenger traffic during summer, and flights to Beirut were resumed that year before being discontinued later. In 1999, PIA leased five Boeing 747–300s from Cathay Pacific to replace its Boeing 747-200M fleet; these aircraft were painted with a new livery featuring a handwork Pashmina tail on a white body and large Pakistan titles on the front fuselage, a design adopted in the early 1990s but dropped due to copyright issues. The 747–300s retained the new livery with a plain green tail and PIA titles, while other aircraft were repainted in the early 1990s livery. The 9/11 attacks in Afghanistan in 2001 closed Afghan airspace, negatively impacting PIA’s operations. However, after restructuring under new management in April 2001, the airline became profitable again. Between 2000 and 2003, cost per employee dropped by 24%, and lower engineering and maintenance costs improved airline revenue. In July 2002, PIA purchased six Boeing 747–300s, five of which were already on lease, with the sixth arriving shortly after and used primarily on North American and European routes. In October 2002, after ten years without new orders, PIA placed an order for eight Boeing 777 aircraft, including three 777-200ER, two 777-200LR, and three 777-300ER variants, becoming the launch customer for the 777-200LR project. Boeing delivered the first 777-200ER to PIA in January 2004, and a new livery was introduced for the 777-200ERs and applied to most of the fleet. PIA also leased six additional Airbus A310-300s directly from Airbus. On 3 November 2005, PIA ordered seven ATR 42-500s to replace its ageing Fokker F27 Friendship fleet. On 10 November 2005, PIA used its 777-200LR to fly the world’s longest commercial flight, covering 21,000 kilometers from Hong Kong to London in 22 hours and 22 minutes—a record still standing as of late 2019. On 6 December 2005, PIA acquired a new Boeing 777-200ER on a ten-year lease. In the same year, Ayesha Rabia Naveed became the first Pakistani woman to captain a scheduled commercial flight and later captained a flight with the first all-woman crew. On 23 December 2006, PIA took delivery of its first Boeing 777-300ER, with the remaining aircraft delivered in January 2007. On 25 February 2006, Boeing delivered its first 777-200LR to PIA. ATR delivered two of the seven ATR 42s in May and December 2006, after which PIA ceased using military Lockheed C-130 Hercules for passenger services in northern Pakistan, having previously used them following the PIA Flight 688 accident. Under the supervision of Mr. Syed Shah, PIA initiated the introduction of long-range 777 aircraft, enabling non-stop flights from Toronto to Karachi, Islamabad, and Lahore beginning 3 March 2006. This strategic move allowed more efficient and seamless travel for passengers and positioned PIA as a prominent player in aviation. However, PIA had planned non-stop flights to New York City, Chicago, Washington, and Houston, which were denied by US authorities due to security concerns after 9/11 unless a European stopover was included. In July 2006, a PIA flight from Multan crashed, killing 45; a government inquiry blamed aging aircraft. Houston services ended in 2006. On 5 March 2007, the European Commission banned 33 of PIA’s 42 aircraft from flying to Europe due to safety concerns over aging planes, though the Boeing 777 fleet was exempted; by that time, 15 aircraft were over 20 years old. PIA argued the ban was discriminatory and unjustifiable. The ban was lifted after four months on 5 July 2007 following an EU Air Safety Administration inspection, with five Boeing 747-300s and six Airbus A310-300s allowed to resume operations. On 29 November 2007, the EU fully lifted the ban, permitting PIA’s entire fleet to fly to Europe. In 2010, PIA changed its livery, replacing the tail with a larger Pakistan national flag and adding "Pakistan International" in gold beneath the PIA logo on the fuselage, with a modified green stripe extended to the rear. By 2011, PIA became unprofitable again and required government subsidies. In 2014, PIA leased four Boeing 737-800s and issued a request for tender for four Boeing 777-300ERs, though the bids were not accepted. The airline leased Airbus A320 aircraft, inducted two A320-214s in 2014, and added two wet-leased A320-211s on 11 August 2014. In October 2014, PIA wet-leased three Boeing 737-800s and accepted bids to dry lease five ATR 72–500s for eight years. In 2015, the last of PIA’s Boeing 747-300s were phased out. In early 2016, PIA was grounded for a week as employees walked out en masse following the deaths of two employees in a protest against privatisation. In August 2016, PIA launched a "Premier Service" to London using an Airbus A330-300 wet-leased from SriLankan Airlines, which was returned after six months and the service discontinued. By the end of 2016, the airline had $3 billion in debt. In January 2017, PIA retired all Airbus A310-300s and leased four Boeing 737-800s from Pegasus Airlines, which were returned after the lease ended. After over 50 years of service, PIA ended its service to New York in October 2017 due to TSA regulations preventing nonstop flights between Pakistan and the US, leaving Toronto as the only North American destination, served by nonstop flights from Karachi, Lahore, and Islamabad. In 2017, PIA replaced its Sabre reservation system with a Turkish-origin system called Hitit, successfully switching to the new system in September 2018. By the end of 2018, the airline had $3.3 billion in debt, up from $2.97 billion the prior year, requiring government bailouts. With the closure of Shaheen Air, PIA launched routes previously served only by Shaheen. In 2019, new profitable routes were launched, and profitable routes like Karachi-Toronto saw increased frequencies, while six unprofitable routes were discontinued. In April 2019, PIA reported that its revenues nearly matched operating costs. Following a visit by TSA officials to Islamabad International Airport in July 2019, PIA expressed hope that non-stop flights to the US would be permitted. In August 2019, PIA laid off 1,000 employees. In September 2019, PIA announced plans to lease additional aircraft to increase its fleet to 37 by 2020 and 45 by 2023. By the end of 2019, PIA reported a 41% year-on-year revenue increase due to route adjustments, reintroduction of grounded aircraft, and higher cargo space utilization. For the first time in its history, PIA operated a relief flight from Lahore to Melbourne during the COVID-19 pandemic. On 22 May 2020, a PIA Airbus A320-214 (AP-BLD) crashed near Karachi airport while en route from Lahore; Flight PK8303, carrying 91 passengers and eight crew members, crashed during descent to Jinnah International Airport, killing 97 and leaving two survivors. The crash was caused by damage from a first belly landing, with both engines flaming out during a go-around. The final report cited human error, non-adherence to SOPs, disregard of ATC instructions, and lack of communication between ATC and the flight crew. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) expressed concerns over "serious lapses in licensing and safety oversight" by the aviation regulator. In November 2020, PIA shut down its courier arm, SpeedEx, which had infrastructure across 74 domestic destinations, and laid off 320 employees. In December 2020, PIA announced plans to lay off half its employees and transferred its engineering arm, Precision Engineering Complex (PEC), to the Pakistan Air Force. On 24 June 2020, following the Flight 8303 crash, Aviation Minister Ghulam Sarwar Khan stated that 262 of Pakistan’s 860 licensed pilots had suspicious or fake licenses, suspected of paying others to take their certification exams. PIA grounded 150 of its 434 pilots and later terminated employment of seven pilots. Almost a week later, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) suspended PIA’s authorization, banning flights in European airspace for six months. On 9 July 2020, the US banned PIA over pilot certification concerns, and the airline was also banned from flying in the UK; Pakistani pilots in Vietnam and Malaysia were temporarily grounded. On 15 July 2020, the US Federal Aviation Administration downgraded Pakistan’s International Aviation Safety Assessment to Category 2, preventing Pakistani airlines from establishing new US services or using US codes. On 18 July 2020, PIA dismissed seven pilots and one cabin crew member whose licenses were revoked by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA). On 28 December 2020, the EU extended its ban for three months, requiring an official CAA inspection. On 16 March 2021, the ban was extended to July, and then to indefinitely on 24 March 2021 following a safety concern about the CAA reported by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), which had not yet conducted a safety audit of the CAA. EASA stated that ICAO’s audit would indicate improvement. On 6 November 2021, the CAA received positive feedback from Europe’s Safety Audit for Foreign-Origin Aircraft (SAFA). In late 2023, PIA was forced to cancel numerous flights due to unpaid fuel bills, leading to customer anger and viral social media content. Pakistan State Oil suspended fueling of PIA aircraft after the airline’s request for additional government funding was denied. On 8 March 2023, PIA completed an online safety audit conducted by EASA. On 29 November 2024, EASA lifted its ban on PIA, citing improvements in the CAA’s oversight, and PIA announced the resumption of flights to Europe, beginning with a flight to Paris on 10 January 2025. However, after advertising the event, PIA apologised for using imagery reminiscent of the September 11 attacks, prompting Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to announce an inquiry. In late December 2023, the Interim government announced a plan to privatise PIA, with Air Marshal (Retd) Farhat Hussain Khan stating that privatisation would occur under the government’s policy to privatise loss-making entities, initially as a flight entity with decisions on other properties to be made later. On 6 January 2025, PIA announced plans to expand its destinations to the Middle East using its Boeing 777 and Airbus A320 fleets. Starting 20 January 2025, PIA began two weekly flights between Sialkot and Bahrain, two weekly flights between Lahore and Dammam, and a once-a-week flight between Lahore and Kuwait. Additionally, weekly flights from Faisalabad to Jeddah and Sialkot to Doha, Qatar began on 20 and 21 January 2025, respectively. On 16 July 2025, the UK’s Civil Aviation Authority lifted its ban on PIA, citing safety improvements. PIA announced plans to resume flights to the UK with three weekly flights between Islamabad and Manchester, later reduced to two weekly. The inaugural flight was delayed due to delays in obtaining necessary approvals.

On 6 January 2025, Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) announced it would expand its operations to the Middle East by introducing weekly flights using its Boeing 777 and Airbus A320 fleets. Starting 20 January 2025, two weekly flights began between Sialkot and Bahrain, and two weekly flights were launched between Lahore and Dammam, with an additional once-a-week flight starting on 25 January 2025 between Lahore and Kuwait. Weekly services from Faisalabad to Jeddah began on 20 January 2025, and a weekly flight from Sialkot to Doha, Qatar, commenced on 21 January 2025. On 16 July 2025, the UK's Civil Aviation Authority lifted its ban on PIA, citing safety improvements, and PIA announced plans to resume flights to the UK with three weekly flights between Islamabad and Manchester, later reduced to two weekly flights. Despite delays in obtaining a Third Country Operator certificate, the certificate was finally secured on 24 September 2025, and flights to the UK commenced in October 2025. On 23 December 2025, a consortium led by the Arif Habib Corporation was awarded a 75% majority stake in PIA through an auction offering 135 billion rupees ($482 million), with Fauji Fertilizer joining the consortium. PIA remains majority-owned by the Government of Pakistan (86%), with 14% held by private shareholders, and is administered by the Aviation Division under a president and chief executive officer, along with a board of nine independent non-executive members. The board has four sub-committees: Audit, Brand and Advertising, Finance, and Human Resource, each with a charter and chairman. The airline’s main headquarters are in Karachi, with smaller offices in several Pakistani cities. Seven of PIA’s ten departments are located in Islamabad—Marketing, Procedure Bureau, Central Reservation Control, Revenue Management, HR and Security and Vigilance—while the remaining three are in Karachi: finance, engineering, and situation room. In the late 1990s, the government proposed privatization due to persistent losses, but plans were not implemented; in 1997, a team from International Finance Corporation (IFC) was brought in for restructuring, but no agreement was reached. On 18 February 2009, PIA was removed from the privatization list. In 2013, the government attempted privatization by selling 26% of shares and management control, but the plan was abandoned after protests following the killing of two employees at Jinnah International Airport. In 2018, the new government decided against privatization and instead focused on profitability through management changes. On 6 February 2024, the interim government decided to split PIA into two entities: TopCo, which handles engineering, ground handling, flight kitchen, and training, and HoldCo, which manages Precision Engineering Complex, PIA Investment Limited, and subordinate departments and properties. On 4 June 2024, six companies—Air Blue, Arif Habib Corporation, Blue World City, Fly Jinnah, Pak Ethanol (Pvt) Consortium, and YB Holdings Consortium—were pre-qualified to bid for PIA’s privatization. On 30 October 2024, only Blue World City submitted a bid, offering 10 billion Pakistani rupees ($36 million) for a 60% stake, significantly below the government’s minimum of 85 billion rupees. On 13 November 2024, the government officially rejected the bid, stating the process would follow laws and regulations with decisions made in the national interest by the cabinet committee. On 9 July 2025, the government approved four potential investors: Air Blue, Fauji Fertilizers, Lucky Cement Consortium (including Hub Power, Kohat Cement, and Metro Ventures), and Arif Habib Consortium (including Fatima Fertilizer, City Schools, and Lake City Holdings). In December 2025, the Government of Pakistan sold its 75% stake in PIA to the Arif Habib-led consortium for 135 billion Pakistani rupees ($480 million), part of a long-delayed privatization linked to broader economic reforms. PIA became unprofitable in 2011, requiring government subsidies, and by the end of 2016, it carried $3 billion in debt, rising to $3.3 billion by the end of 2018, necessitating government bailouts. In April 2019, PIA reported that revenues nearly matched operating costs; an audit revealed 46 empty flights between 2016 and 2017, resulting in a $1.1 million loss, and 36 Hajj flights without passengers. By the end of 2019, PIA reported a 41% year-on-year revenue increase due to route rationalization, reintroduction of idle aircraft, and increased cargo utilization. PIA faces profitability challenges due to "capacity dumping" by Middle East airlines, such as Emirates operating up to seven daily flights to Karachi on high-capacity Boeing 777s under Pakistan’s Open Skies Agreement with the UAE. PIA discontinued profitable US routes due to TSA restrictions requiring costly diversions to European airports, and new routes to Najaf and Bangkok did not improve finances due to seasonality. Staffing issues, including an employee count of 18,014 in 2010 for a 40-aircraft fleet, remain a challenge, though 1,000 employees were laid off in August 2019. As of November 2019, PIA served 19 domestic and 28 international destinations across 20 countries in Asia, the Middle East, Europe, and North America. Through interline agreements and codeshare partnerships, PIA offers travel options in 102 international destinations across 40 countries. PIA’s hubs are Jinnah International Airport, Allama Iqbal International Airport, and Islamabad International Airport, with Karachi as the main hub and Islamabad and Lahore as secondary hubs. PIA has codeshare and interline agreements with various airlines and cargo special pro-rate agreements with others. As of December 2025, PIA operates a fleet of aircraft, with the government requiring 38 new aircraft over four years; the new owner, Arif Habib Consortium, plans to add 38 aircraft in the first phase and 65 in the second phase over four to six years. In December 2003, PIA introduced a new livery on its first Boeing 777-200ER and two leased Airbus A310s, featuring a white front and beige rear with a dark green stripe, a white tail with a dark green PIA acronym, and a raised "Pakistan" title; due to criticism, the design was modified, replacing the tail logo with a flowing Pakistan flag on beige, removing "Pakistan" titles, and enlarging the PIA acronym. In early 2006, four provincial tail designs were launched—Sindh, Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Balochistan—each featuring cultural motifs and a city name, but were discontinued in 2009 due to high costs. In mid-April 2010, a new livery was launched featuring a green and gold strip down the fuselage and tail, white forward and off-white/beige rear, a large wavy Pakistan flag on the tail, and "PIA" in dark green and "Pakistan" in golden letters at the front. In July 2014, a "crescent and star" was introduced on the engine cowlings in place of the Urdu logo; in 2015, the 1960s livery was applied to three A320s and one Boeing 777-200ER. In April 2018, PIA launched a new brand identity with a Markhor, Pakistan’s national animal, on aircraft, symbolizing resilience, grace, and fortitude, with a forward leaping Markhor on the tail and two on the engines; however, the Supreme Court of Pakistan issued a suo motu notice halting the rebranding due to concerns over staff salaries, later allowing retention of the flag on the tail and dismissing the case, but the rebranding was ultimately abandoned. Currently, PIA operates a hybrid livery with a euro-white fuselage, gold Urdu logo at front exits and engine cowls, and retains the flag tail, English and Pakistan titles in dark green on the belly, and the PIA corporate website ahead of the aft exits. Five Boeing 777s and three A320s currently feature this livery. PIA Catering supplies meals at Islamabad and Karachi, producing 15,000 meals daily; flight kitchens were managed by Singapore Air Terminal Services (SATS) from 2006 to 2011, after which PIA managed them independently. In April 2019, an MOU was signed with McDonald’s for catering, and PIA provides special meals for dietary and religious needs, with no alcoholic beverages or pork served due to Islamic dietary laws. PIA Premier, a luxury service launched on 14 August 2016 using an A330 wet-leased from SriLankan Airlines, operated six weekly flights to London and three each from Islamabad and Lahore, but was discontinued due to a loss of 2.1 billion rupees. PIA was the first international airline to introduce a regularly scheduled film on board in 1962. In January 2017, PIA began trials of an on-board internet system for domestic flights, allowing passengers to access content via their mobile devices; Boeing 777s offer personal screens with movies, music, TV, maps, and air shows, and selected A320s have drop-down screens with maps and air shows. The Precision Engineering Complex (PEC), originally a PIA subsidiary, produces high-precision components for aerospace and engineering, with capabilities in investment casting, CNC machining, optics, PCB manufacturing, electronics, and composites, and is a supplier to General Electric, Airbus, and Boeing. In late 2025, ownership of PEC was transferred from PIAHCL to Precision Engineering Complex (Private) Limited, a company under the Pakistan Air Force, as part of the government-led restructuring and privatization effort.

The Precision Engineering Complex (PEC) is a specialized manufacturing and engineering facility that was originally part of Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) and later became a subsidiary of the Pakistan International Airlines Holding Company Limited (PIAHCL). It is now owned by Precision Engineering Complex (Private) Limited, a company designated by the Pakistan Air Force, following an ownership transfer approved by PIAHCL shareholders in late 2025 as part of the government-led restructuring and privatization of the national flag carrier. The PEC is an integrated complex that produces high-precision components for the aerospace and broader engineering industries, with capabilities in investment casting, conventional and CNC machining, optics, PCB manufacturing, electrical, electronics, and composites. It holds international certifications and serves as a supplier to major global aerospace companies such as General Electric, Airbus Industries, and Boeing. PIA provides ground handling services to various airlines, operates PIA Cargo—a cargo airline that transports goods across Pakistan and internationally, including meat packing, vegetables, textiles, paper products, laboratory equipment, and postal mail—and previously operated Air Express in the 1970s, launching a dedicated cargo division in 1974 using two Boeing 707-320C aircraft, which operated to the Middle East and Europe before ending in the late 1990s. From 2004 to 2007, it operated two Airbus A300 Freighter aircraft chartered through MNG Airlines to Haan, Luton, Amsterdam, Basel, and Cologne, before discontinuing the service. In 2003, PIA launched PIA Speedex, a courier service initially in four cities that expanded to twelve within a year and now serves over 70 locations in Pakistan, collecting and delivering shipments from customers' homes. In 2019, the new PIA management increased cargo space utilization from 20 percent to nearly 80 percent. PIA currently offers cargo services to international destinations including Abu Dhabi, Bangkok, Barcelona, Birmingham, Beijing, Copenhagen, Doha, Dubai, Jeddah, Kabul, Kuala Lumpur, London, Manchester, Medina, Milan, Muscat, Najaf, Oslo, Paris, Riyadh, Sharjah, Tokyo–Narita, and Toronto–Canada. The airline sponsors various events domestically and abroad, including the three green stripe livery introduced in the 1990s to support sports, backing the PIA first-class cricket team in the Quaid-i-Azam Trophy and Patron's Trophy, the PIA football club, the A1 Team Pakistan in the A1 Grand Prix, and the annual Shandur Polo Gala in northern Pakistan. PIA has had a sports division since 1958, promoting cricket, hockey, football, squash, polo, tennis, bridge, chess, table tennis, cycling, and bodybuilding. It also operates a Boy Scouts Association (PIA-BSA) in partnership with the Pakistan Boy Scouts Association, which provided relief after the 2005 earthquake. PIA was an official sponsor of "Destination Pakistan 2007" and in 2008 partnered with Ufone to offer air miles to mobile network users, and with Standard Chartered Bank to launch air miles credit cards. In 2009, it was the gold sponsor of Logistics Pakistan and formed a strategic alliance with the Pakistan Remittance Initiative (PRI) to promote international money transfers. PIA operates planetariums in Karachi and Lahore featuring static aircraft and astronomy shows, and PIA Horticulture, established in 1996, supplies flowers for offices and events, winning awards nationally. The airline supports non-profit organizations such as Al-Shifa Trust, Zindagi Trust, The Citizens Foundation, and Sindh Institute of Urology and Transplantation. In 2009, it partnered with McDonald's to offer meal discounts and upgrades. PIA owns three hotels—Roosevelt Hotel, Scribe Hotel, and Skyrooms (Private) Limited—and has an agreement with Pearl Continental Hotels for UAE-based passengers. PIA has continuously transported government officials, including the President and Prime Minister, on overseas visits; during the late 1990s, a Boeing 737–300 was used for official trips, later transferred permanently to PIA after a military coup in 1999, and subsequently replaced by two Airbus A310-300s. In February 2007, Qatar gifted an Airbus A310 to the Pakistani government, ending the need for PIA aircraft for official travel, though occasional use of PIA's Airbus A320 or Boeing 777 is still made. PIA operates private charter flights using ATR 42s to Bhit, Kadanwari, and Sehwan Sharif in Sindh and other domestic locations for oil and gas companies and customers, and provides ad hoc charters for United Nations peacekeeping troops to Africa, Eastern Europe, Asia (South Korea, Afghanistan, Tajikistan, East Timor), and other international destinations through its Charter Team. The airline runs a two-month Hajj operation annually to Saudi Arabia, transporting over 100,000 pilgrims until its fleet reduced to 25 aircraft in 2011–2012, after which the Hajj quota was reduced to 60,000 to 70,000 pilgrims. On 27 September 2024, PIA received Pakistan's first National Tourism Award for Promoting Travel and Tourism, awarded to Air Vice Marshal Amir Hayat, CEO of PIA, in recognition of its efforts in promoting domestic travel. The airline has experienced more than 30 aircraft losses, including 20 fatal crashes, and has been involved in at least eight hijacking incidents between 1971 and 2017.
